20

21

12 REQUEST FOR ORDER OF MOTION (FAMILY LAW GENERIC) BOARDING SCHOOL/SCHOOL
13 CHOICE, SANCTIONS
14 TENTATIVE RULING
15 Having read and considered the pleadings, declarations, and other evidence submitted in this matter, the
16 Court makes the following findings and orders:
17 BACKGROUND AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY.
18 Petitioner, Kevin Pluim, filed his present Request for Order on October 27, 2025. In it he is
19 requesting that the Court assist the parties with choosing the high school that their son, Oliver, would be
20 attending beginning the fall semester of 2026. Petitioner/Father’s desire that their son be given the
21 opportunity to attend a boarding school had been raised by him before. Petitioner filed a request
22 previously on March 20, 2025 which was followed by numerous pleadings and was finally heard on June
23 12, 2025. The Court’s Ruling on the Request was filed on June 26, 2025.
24 According to the Court’s Ruling, Father had requested that Oliver be permitted to attend a
25 boarding school, that is, any boarding school in the United States that would accept him, and per Oliver’s
26 preference. Father indicated he believed that attending a boarding school would be in Oliver’s best
27 interest. The Court was not persuaded. As stated, the Court found that Father had failed in his burden to
28 prove that attending a boarding school would be in Oliver’s best interest; that it appeared from the
29 evidence presented that Oliver had a stable life and a stable academic plan. Further, the Court’s Ruling
1 indicated that it was "unable to make a finding that it would be in Oliver’s best interest to attend an
2 unknown school in an unknown location which has not even been identified for the Court”.
3 Respondent/Mother has argued in her pleadings that this Court should once again deny Father’s
4 request. She claims that nothing has materially changed since the last time Father brought this request
5 and it was denied, that Oliver continues to do well where he is, and that he has established a peer
6 community and close friendships that should not be disrupted.
7 Although the parties cannot agree on the resolution, there appears to be no dispute regarding the
8 facts. They agree on the following:
9 1. Since the last Court Ruling Oliver has been given the opportunity to explore Stevenson School, a
10 boarding school located in Pebble Beach, California, including three tours, two with Father and
11 one with Mother.
12 2. He has completed his application, gone through the interview process, and attended an
13 admissions event.
14 3. Oliver has expressed a desire to attend Stevenson School this coming fall to both his mother and
15 his father. Both parents have informed themselves as fully as possible about the program and the
16 opportunities for Oliver.
17 4. Both parents have heard Oliver state that he would prefer to discontinue the back-and-forth
18 between his parents’ households now that his older brother will be going away to college, and
19 instead to settle in at a boarding school.
20 5. They both understand the opportunities Oliver would have to continue to pursue his love of
21 sports, particularly golf and soccer, while attending Stevenson. They also agree that Oliver has
22 been very engaged in soccer while attending his current middle school, including competitive
23 teams.
24 6. Admissions/acceptance will be decided March 20, 2026.
25 7. Both parents have also explored Stuart Hall as another option which is a private high school in
26 San Francisco.
27 Mother, in her pleadings, states that, in her opinion, Oliver needs the “stability” of attending a
28 local private high school where he can continue to “benefit” from daily contact with a parent on his
29
1 current week-on-week-off schedule, and maintain his friendships. She does not think that his preference
2 to attend Stevenson is well reasoned and is perhaps more an emotional reaction to his brother’s leaving.
3 Father disagrees and asks the Court to allow Oliver to speak for himself to the court. He wants
4 the Court to give Oliver a chance to attend Stevenson, if accepted. He indicates that he would be open to
5 reconsidering the decision after one year if it turns out to be something that doesn’t work for Oliver. He
6 also believes that Stevenson is close enough to San Francisco that Oliver’s stabile relationships with
7 family and friends can be maintained through weekend experiences.
8 The parties have been to mediation twice and are still unable to reach agreement on a choice of
9 school.
10 FINDING AND ORDERS
11 1. Petitioner’s objections and request to strike:
12 Petitioner filed a list of five objections, two are hearsay, and those are granted. The other three are on
13 the basis of “speculation”. Those pertain to statements made by Mother in her Declaration that
14 express her opinion about her son, Oliver. It is patently clear that the parties do not share the same
15 opinions about what may or may not be “good” for the child. While they are not expert child
16 psychologists, they should be entitled to the same leeway that the law allows in permitting one to
17 opine on the value of property that one owns. The Court gives equal weight to the opinions of both
18 parties. Those objections are denied.
19 2. The Court agrees with Father’s legal arguments regarding his burden when bringing this request to
20 the court for the second time. First, the Court specifically stated in its prior Ruling that the issue of
21 the reduction of frequency of contact with parents which it felt to be potentially burdensome to the
22 child could be somewhat lessened if he were to attend a school closer to home, “like Stevenson
23 School in Carmel”. The circumstances under which Father brings this Request now are different than
24 those that were presented to the Court previously, as the parents have more concrete information to
25 provide the court, and the child has expressed a preference and opinion with reasons. The child’s
26 expression of his position is undisputed by either parent.
27 3. Oliver is completing eighth grade and will be matriculating from his present school. Like his other
28 classmates, decisions have to be made as to where he will go to school in the fall. Wherever he goes,
29
1 some of his friends may go there too, but others may go somewhere else. He will be introduced to
2 new people and a new campus no matter where he goes.
3 4. Mother argues that “frequent and continuing contact” with both parents is essential to his wellbeing.
4 The Court agrees but believes that, at this phase of Oliver’s life other considerations should be given
5 at least equal weight. The law requires that the Court consider what Oliver wants, and his voice has
6 been made clear to the Court without the need for him to actually come and tell the Court himself.
7 5. The Court finds that it would be in Oliver’s best interest to allow him to benefit and learn from the
8 exercise of his own judgment. He has explored the location and his academic and extracurricular
9 opportunities at Stevenson School. He has spent time with people there. He has done his research.
10 He has weighed the benefits and burdens of continuing his current parenting schedule without the
11 support and company of his older sibling versus the boarding school experience. He asks for the
12 opportunity to give it a try.
13 6. The Court has also considered the fact that the decision is not immutable, and that, if need be, it can
14 be reconsidered if it does not go well for Oliver. Oliver will still have been given the opportunity to
15 learn consequences of decisions and how to evaluate and make better decisions in the future. This too
16 is in his best interest.
17 ORDER
18 1. Father’s Request for Oliver to attend Stevenson School if accepted is granted.
19 2. Both parties’ requests for Family Code section 271 sanctions are denied.
20 3. A future hearing date is set for Thursday, 4/9/2026 at 9:00 AM in Dept. 404. At least 10 calendar
21 days prior to the next hearing date, both parties shall file and serve declarations providing any
22 material updates to the Court.
23 4. Father’s attorney shall prepare the Findings and Order After Hearing.
24 5. Preparation of Order: If you are directed by the court to prepare the order after hearing – within 10
25 calendar days of the hearing you must either: (a) Serve the proposed order to the other party/counsel
26 for approval, and follow the procedures set forth in CA Rules of Court, Rule 5.125(c), or (b) If the
27 other party did not appear or the matter was uncontested, submit the proposed order after hearing
28 directly to the court. Failure to submit the order after hearing within 10 days may allow the other
29
1 party to prepare a proposed order and submit it to the court in accordance with CA Rules of Court,
2 Rule 5.125(d).
